subtopic_detail: Symptomatic anterior vaginal wall descent to the hymen in an 82 year old declined for anaesthesia because of severe respiratory disease
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing an 82 year old woman who describes a dragging feeling and a bulge she can feel at the entrance to the vagina by the end of each day. It is worse after she has been gardening and eases when she lies down.

She has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on home oxygen and was assessed by the anaesthetic clinic last month as unsuitable for a general or regional anaesthetic. She has completed three months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist without improvement. She is sexually inactive, has had no bleeding, and her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago. Examination shows anterior wall descent reaching the hymen on straining with well oestrogenised tissue.

data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descending to the level of the hymen on Valsalva, cervix descending to 2 cm above the hymen, no posterior compartment defect, vaginal epithelium moist and rugated with no ulceration, no adnexal mass, post void residual volume 40 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fit a ring pessary in the clinic and review her in the clinic within six weeks
options.rationale: A mechanical support inserted in the outpatient setting relieves the symptoms of descent without an anaesthetic, which is the decisive consideration when she has already been declared unfit for theatre, and a supported first review checks for erosion and retention. Conservative therapy has already been given an adequate trial. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior repair on the next elective list
options.rationale: Reconstructive surgery is the definitive option for descent that fails conservative management, and it is exactly what the anaesthetic assessment has excluded for this woman. Offering it ignores the risk that ended the surgical pathway last month. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Prescribe a further six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training now
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training is first line for mild descent and for symptoms without a visible bulge, but a documented three month supervised programme without benefit has already tested that option. Repeating a failed intervention delays symptom relief without changing the anatomy. (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia: Pelvic organ prolapse)
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream alone and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen improves tissue quality and is often used alongside a pessary, but her epithelium is already moist and rugated so there is no atrophy to reverse. It does not support a descended anterior wall by itself. (Source: Australian Menopause Society: Vaginal oestrogen)

options.text: Refer for colpocleisis under local infiltration on the next available theatre list
options.rationale: Obliterative surgery is a genuine option for an older woman who is not sexually active and is a poor candidate for reconstruction, so the near pair question is whether any theatre procedure should precede a clinic fitted device. It still requires an anaesthetic and is considered only after a pessary trial fails. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ descent is present in about half of parous women on examination but only a minority have symptoms, and the symptom that correlates best with the anatomy is the sensation of a bulge. Management runs from lifestyle measures and supervised pelvic floor training for mild symptoms, through vaginal pessaries, to reconstructive or obliterative surgery. A pessary is not merely a holding measure for those awaiting theatre, since a substantial proportion of women continue with one indefinitely by preference, and it is the option of choice for anyone who is unfit for anaesthesia, still planning a pregnancy, or simply declines surgery. Ongoing review is part of the treatment because a neglected device erodes into the vaginal wall.
key_points: The sensation of a bulge is the symptom that tracks the anatomy
Supervised pelvic floor training is first line for mild symptomatic descent
A pessary is definitive therapy in its own right, not only a bridge to surgery
Anaesthetic unfitness moves a pessary ahead of all surgical options
Regular review prevents vaginal erosion and unrecognised retention
explanation.pearls: A woman fitted with a ring pessary should be reviewed within six weeks and then every six months, and topical vaginal oestrogen is usually added because it reduces the rate of erosion in atrophic tissue that is in continuous contact with silicone.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Frequent prolonged unscheduled bleeding five months after insertion of a progestogen implant in a woman who wants to keep the device
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who had a contraceptive implant placed in her upper arm five months ago. She has bled on more days than not since, with episodes lasting eight to ten days, and she has had enough of it but says she does not want to go back to remembering a daily tablet.

She has no pain, no postcoital bleeding and no discharge, and she is in a new relationship since the implant was inserted. Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. A urine pregnancy test today is negative and a self collected swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is negative. Speculum and bimanual examination are normal and the implant is palpable in the correct plane.

data_table.Examination: Implant palpable subdermally in the medial upper left arm, cervix healthy with no contact bleeding, uterus anteverted and normal size, adnexae non-tender with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, self collected vaginal swab negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, haemoglobin 129 g/L (115-155), ferritin 38 micrograms per litre (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her bleeding?

options.text: Remove the implant today and arrange insertion of a hormonal intrauterine device
options.rationale: Switching to an intrauterine system is a reasonable eventual step if medical treatment fails, but removing the device at the first review discards a highly effective method before any treatment has been tried. She has also asked to keep long acting contraception rather than change it now. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Reassure her that the pattern will settle and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Bleeding patterns established by three months predict the pattern for the remaining life of the device, so waiting a further three months is unlikely to change anything. Unscheduled bleeding is the commonest reason for early removal, and untreated it usually ends the method. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Offer a three month course of a combined oral contraceptive alongside the implant
options.rationale: Once pregnancy, infection and a cervical cause have been excluded, a three month course of combined oestrogen and progestogen taken alongside the device is the best supported treatment for troublesome unscheduled bleeding and settles it in most women while the implant stays in place. It directly meets her wish to keep long acting cover. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid to be taken continuously for the next three months
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic treatment reduces the volume of heavy scheduled menstrual loss, and the near pair here is that her problem is the frequency and duration of bleeding rather than the volume. It is also not used continuously for months at a time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and an endometrial biopsy before any other treatment
options.rationale: Structural assessment and sampling belong to women over 45, those with risk factors for endometrial pathology, or those whose bleeding persists after treatment. In a 24 year old with a normal examination and negative swabs the yield is effectively nil. (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal uterine bleeding)

explanation.summary: About one in five women using a progestogen implant has frequent or prolonged unscheduled bleeding, and it is by far the commonest reason the device is removed early. The assessment is short and specific: exclude pregnancy, test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, check that cervical screening is up to date, and examine the cervix, because a new relationship or a cervical lesion changes the answer entirely. When that work up is clear, the bleeding reflects a thin unstable endometrium under continuous progestogen rather than any pathology. A three month course of combined hormonal treatment is the best supported medical option, with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory as an alternative, and women should be told before insertion that the pattern is unpredictable so that it is not a surprise.
key_points: Unscheduled bleeding is the leading reason for early implant removal
Exclude pregnancy, chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and a cervical cause first
The pattern at three months predicts the pattern for the device's life
A three month combined hormonal course is the best supported treatment
Structural imaging is reserved for older women or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Counselling before insertion that about one in five women will bleed unpredictably and one in five will have no bleeding at all substantially reduces early removal rates, because most discontinuation is driven by surprise rather than by the volume of blood lost.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Sixteen year old requesting the three monthly progestogen injection whose mother has raised concerns about bone strength
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16 year old who has come in with her mother asking for the contraceptive injection because her friend uses it and she does not want anything she has to think about. She has regular periods, no medical problems and takes no medication.

Her mother has read that the injection weakens bones and wants to know whether her daughter should have a bone density scan first. She eats normally, plays netball twice a week and has never had a fracture. She is competent to consent and has discussed the decision with you alone as well as with her mother present. Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre, her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, no features of an eating disorder, secondary sexual characteristics fully developed, general examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice and management?

options.text: Decline the injection because of her age and offer the combined pill as an alternative
options.rationale: Adolescence is not a contraindication to this method in Australian practice, and refusing the method she will actually use in favour of a daily tablet predictably raises her risk of an unintended pregnancy. The combined pill remains a reasonable option if she chooses it, not a substitute for her decision. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Arrange a dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan before the first injection is given
options.rationale: Bone densitometry is not recommended before or during use of this method because the reference ranges are not validated in adolescents and the result would not change management in a healthy young woman. It medicalises a reversible effect and delays contraception. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give the injection now and plan to stop the method after two years of continuous use
options.rationale: A fixed two year ceiling was once advised but current Australian guidance is to review the choice periodically rather than to impose a stopping date, since density recovers after discontinuation. A scheduled stop can leave a young woman without effective cover for no measured benefit. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Give the injection now, with advice on calcium, vitamin D and weight bearing exercise
options.rationale: Age alone does not restrict this method, and the small reversible fall in bone mineral density recovers after the injections stop, so the balance in an adolescent at risk of an unintended pregnancy favours giving it with bone healthy advice. Efficacy and her preference for a method she does not have to remember both support proceeding. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Give the injection now and add a daily oestrogen tablet to protect her bone density
options.rationale: Adding oestrogen for bone protection alone is not supported and exposes her to thrombotic risk for no proven gain. The near pair is that combined hormonal treatment is used for bleeding problems on progestogen only methods, which is a different indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

explanation.summary: The three monthly injectable progestogen suppresses ovulation and produces a modest fall in bone mineral density that is greatest in the first two years of use, is largest in adolescents who are still accruing peak bone mass, and reverses after the method is stopped. No study has shown an increase in fracture risk attributable to the method, so Australian guidance does not restrict it by age and does not impose a maximum duration. The practical response to a family's concern is accurate information plus attention to the things that genuinely build bone, namely adequate calcium and vitamin D, weight bearing exercise and avoidance of smoking. Return of fertility is delayed by a median of several months after the last injection, which is a more common practical issue than bone density.
key_points: Bone density falls modestly and recovers after the method is stopped
No increase in fracture risk has been demonstrated for this method
Age under 18 is not a contraindication in Australian practice
Densitometry before or during use is not recommended
Return of fertility is delayed by a median of several months
explanation.pearls: Fertility returns a median of nine months after the last injection, so a woman who may want to conceive within a year should be steered towards a method with immediate reversibility such as an implant or an intrauterine device.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Painful glazed erosions at the vestibule with a lacy white border and oral changes in a woman failing topical steroid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman with eighteen months of vulval soreness and burning that makes intercourse impossible. She describes rawness rather than itch and says the skin feels like it is peeling.

Her general practitioner has treated her for thrush three times and then prescribed a potent topical corticosteroid ointment for eight weeks, which helped a little but never cleared it. She has also had sore gums for the past year and her dentist has commented on white streaks inside her cheeks. She has hypothyroidism on thyroxine. Examination shows glazed red erosions at the vestibule with a fine white lacy margin, loss of the labia minora, and narrowing of the introitus.

data_table.Examination: Glazed erythematous erosions around the vestibule with a reticulate white border, resorption of the labia minora, introital narrowing admitting one finger with discomfort, no thickened white plaques over the perianal skin, buccal mucosa with bilateral white lacy striae, vaginal walls erythematous with a serous discharge
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab negative for candida and bacterial vaginosis, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take a vulval biopsy from the centre of an erosion and stop all topical treatment
options.rationale: A biopsy through the floor of an erosion yields only ulcer slough without the epidermal changes the pathologist needs. Stopping treatment while waiting also allows further scarring of an introitus that is already narrowed. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval lichen planus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval lichen planus

options.text: Prescribe a further course of oral fluconazole and repeat the vaginal swab afterwards
options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis causes itch with curdy discharge and responds to antifungals, and she has already failed three courses with a negative swab. Continuing to treat an excluded infection is the pattern that delays this diagnosis by years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen alone and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Genitourinary changes after menopause cause dryness and dyspareunia with pale thin tissue, not erosions with a lacy border, and they do not affect the mouth. Oestrogen is a useful adjunct but it will not heal an inflammatory dermatosis. (Source: Australian Menopause Society: Vaginal oestrogen)

options.text: Refer for examination under anaesthesia with surgical division of the narrowed introitus
options.rationale: Surgery to a vulva with active erosive inflammation reliably provokes further scarring and new lesions at the incision, and it is reserved for stable disease that has been medically controlled. The near pair is that adhesiolysis can be appropriate once the dermatosis is quiescent. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Take a vulval biopsy from the edge of an erosion and continue ultrapotent steroid
options.rationale: Erosive disease with a reticulate white border, oral involvement and architectural loss needs histological confirmation because it differs from the commoner white sclerotic condition in treatment, in vaginal involvement and in the need for dilator use. Sampling the edge rather than the base of an erosion gives interpretable tissue while treatment continues. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Chronic vulval symptoms are frequently treated as candidiasis for years before the underlying dermatosis is recognised, and the clue is the absence of itch with a burning raw quality and failure of repeated antifungal courses. Erosive disease of the vulva and vagina is distinguished from the sclerotic white condition by glazed erosions with a lacy reticulate margin, by involvement of the vagina producing a discharge and adhesions, and by mucosal disease elsewhere, especially in the mouth. Histology is worth obtaining because the two conditions differ in management and because both carry a risk of squamous carcinoma at the site. Treatment combines ultrapotent topical corticosteroid to the vulva, intravaginal corticosteroid where the vagina is involved, dilators to preserve the introitus, and specialist input for refractory disease.
key_points: Burning and rawness rather than itch suggests erosive disease
A reticulate white margin and oral striae point away from the sclerotic form
Vaginal involvement with adhesions occurs in the erosive form only
Biopsy the edge of an erosion, never the base
Both vulval dermatoses carry a long term risk of squamous carcinoma
explanation.pearls: The combination of erosive vulval, vaginal and gingival disease defines the vulvovaginal gingival syndrome, and these women need intravaginal corticosteroid plus regular dilator use because vaginal adhesions can obliterate the upper vagina within months of uncontrolled inflammation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval lichen planus

subtopic_detail: Monthly lower abdominal pain for six months with no menarche and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus in a fully developed adolescent
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 14 year old girl referred by her general practitioner with six months of lower abdominal pain that comes for three or four days each month and then goes completely. She has never had a period.

Her breasts developed at 11 and she has full pubic and axillary hair. She has grown 9 cm in the last two years. Over the last fortnight she has also been going to the toilet more often and feeling that she cannot empty her bladder properly. Abdominal examination finds a smooth suprapubic mass rising to just below the umbilicus. Inspection of the introitus shows a tense bluish membrane that bulges when she strains.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, smooth non-tender suprapubic mass palpable to 4 cm below the umbilicus, tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus on Valsalva with no visible vaginal opening, normal external genitalia otherwise, no inguinal masses
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, post void bladder scan 180 mL, pelvic ultrasound showing a distended vagina filled with echogenic fluid and a normal uterus and both ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Arrange needle aspiration of the collection in the clinic under local anaesthesia
options.rationale: Aspiration decompresses the collection temporarily but leaves the obstruction in place so it refills, and puncturing the membrane introduces organisms into retained blood, risking pyocolpos. Definitive drainage requires an adequate opening. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive continuously to suppress further bleeding now
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression stops further accumulation and is used as a holding measure when surgery must be delayed, but it does nothing for the litre of blood already trapped or for the urinary retention it is causing. The near pair is that suppression treats the inflow while surgery treats the obstruction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: Arrange surgical incision and drainage of the obstructed outflow tract in theatre
options.rationale: Cyclical pain with normal secondary sexual development, a distended vagina on imaging and a bulging membrane identifies an obstructed outflow tract, and the treatment is a formal incision of the membrane under anaesthesia with drainage of the retained blood. Doing it in theatre allows adequate excision and prevents restenosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

options.text: Arrange a karyotype and measure gonadotrophins before any procedure is undertaken
options.rationale: Chromosomal and hormonal testing is the pathway for absent menstruation without cyclical pain, where the question is whether a uterus and functioning ovaries exist. Her ultrasound has already shown a normal uterus and ovaries and her pain is cyclical. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any decision on treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when the ultrasound suggests a more complex obstruction such as a transverse septum or a duplicated system, since the surgical approach differs. A thin bulging membrane visible at the introitus with a normal uterus does not need it. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

explanation.summary: An adolescent with normal secondary sexual development, no menstruation and cyclical pain has an obstructed outflow tract until proven otherwise, and the diagnosis is usually made on inspection of the introitus that is too often omitted. Retained menstrual blood distends the vagina and later the uterus and tubes, and the mass can compress the bladder neck to cause urinary frequency or frank retention, or the rectum to cause constipation. Ultrasound confirms a fluid filled vagina with a normal uterus and ovaries, which separates this from absent uterine development or gonadal dysgenesis where there is no cyclical pain. Definitive treatment is surgical incision of the obstructing membrane with drainage, and long term outcomes including fertility are good, although retrograde spill during the years of obstruction gives a higher rate of endometriosis.
key_points: Cyclical pain with absent menstruation signals obstruction, not ovarian failure
Normal breast and pubic hair development indicates functioning ovaries
Urinary frequency or retention reflects mass effect on the bladder neck
Inspection of the introitus makes the diagnosis in most cases
Karyotype and gonadotrophins belong to amenorrhoea without cyclical pain
explanation.pearls: Retained menstrual blood in an obstructed tract refluxes through the tubes, so these girls carry a substantially higher lifetime rate of endometriosis and should be told that persisting pelvic pain after surgery deserves assessment rather than reassurance.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Milky discharge from both breasts with six months of absent periods and a mildly raised prolactin in a woman recently started on an antiemetic
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman who has noticed a milky fluid coming from both nipples when she showers, and who has not had a period for six months. She has never been pregnant.

She has had nausea from gastroparesis for the last eight months and her gastroenterologist started her on domperidone seven months ago, which she takes three times a day. She has no headache and no change in her vision, and she has not gained weight or become constipated. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. Her serum prolactin taken this morning after a rushed walk from the car park is 1180 milliunits per litre.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, breasts otherwise normal with no mass, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features, no goitre, no striae or proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1180 milliunits per litre (less than 500), urine pregnancy test negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), follicle stimulating hormone 4.1 international units per litre, luteinising hormone 3.6 international units per litre, oestradiol 180 picomoles per litre

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast this week
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated once pregnancy, medication, hypothyroidism and renal impairment have been excluded, or immediately if there is headache, visual field loss or a markedly higher level. Imaging now will find incidental lesions in a proportion of normal people and confuse a drug effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start cabergoline twice weekly and review her prolactin level again in eight weeks
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist treats a prolactin secreting adenoma, which has not been demonstrated, and giving it alongside a dopamine antagonist sets the two drugs against each other while worsening her gastroparesis. Treatment precedes diagnosis here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive to restore her periods and review in three months
options.rationale: Restoring a withdrawal bleed masks the marker that is being used to monitor the underlying problem and treats neither the discharge nor its cause. Oestrogen replacement has a place once a cause is established and hypogonadism is expected to persist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Discuss stopping the antiemetic with her gastroenterologist and repeat the prolactin
options.rationale: A dopamine antagonist started one month before the symptoms began is a sufficient explanation for a prolactin at this level, and drug induced elevation is confirmed by the fall after the agent is withdrawn or substituted. Consulting the prescriber keeps her gastric symptoms managed while the test is repeated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange a macroprolactin assay and consider the result sufficient if it is positive
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive complex that explains a raised laboratory value in a woman with no symptoms, and the near pair is that it is the right test for an incidental elevation rather than for a woman with discharge and absent periods. Her symptoms indicate biologically active hormone. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Prolactin testing)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Prolactin testing

explanation.summary: Raised prolactin suppresses gonadotrophin pulsatility, which is why the clinical picture combines milky discharge with absent or infrequent periods and sometimes reduced libido or bone loss. The work up runs pregnancy, medication review, thyroid function and renal function before any imaging, because drugs are the commonest cause outside pregnancy and lactation, with dopamine antagonists, antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, verapamil and oestrogens the usual culprits. Levels also rise transiently with stress, venepuncture, exercise and nipple stimulation, so a modest elevation is repeated on a rested sample before it is acted on. Very high levels of several thousand milliunits per litre, or any level with headache or visual field loss, bypass this sequence and go straight to pituitary imaging.
key_points: Exclude pregnancy, drugs, hypothyroidism and renal failure before imaging
Dopamine antagonists are the commonest drug cause of elevation
Stress, exercise and nipple stimulation raise the level transiently
Headache or visual field loss mandates immediate pituitary imaging
Suppressed gonadotrophins explain the absent periods and low oestradiol
explanation.pearls: A prolactin above about 5000 milliunits per litre nearly always indicates a prolactin secreting adenoma rather than a drug effect, whereas antipsychotics and antiemetics usually produce levels between 1000 and 3000, so the number itself steers whether imaging can wait for a drug washout.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Prolactin testing
